title: How a 90s Power Ballad Made the New Lego Batman Trailer Unforgettable
summary: Picture this: you’re watching a trailer for a Lego Batman game, expecting the usual orchestral swells or maybe some generic rock. Instead, you’re greeted by the unmistakable opening notes of Seal’s “Kiss from a Rose.” It’s unexpected, it’s nostalgic, and it works so perfectly that you might just watch the trailer five times in a row. That’s the magic of the new launch trailer for Lego Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight, released on May 7 by Warner Bros. and TT Games. The game itself is an ambitious open-world spin on the Arkham formula, built entirely from digital Lego bricks. It pulls characters, moments, and vehicles from the Caped Crusader’s entire 80-year history, weaving them into a brand-new story. The trailer’s song choice isn’t just a random throwback — it’s a deep-cut reference. “Kiss from a Rose” originally debuted alongside The NeverEnding Story III in 1994, but it became a global phenomenon when it was re-released on the Batman Forever soundtrack in 1995. By using it, the marketing team signals that this game is a love letter to every era of Batman, from the campy 60s to the gritty Arkham games. The trailer even includes a sly nod to behind-the-scenes drama: a reference to Jim Carrey’s story about how Tommy Lee Jones allegedly hated him on the set of Batman Forever. It’s the kind of joke that will fly over most kids’ heads but land perfectly with adult fans. And that’s the point — the game is designed to charm players of all ages. As Kotaku’s Ethan Gach pointed out, the song’s history adds another layer of cleverness to the trailer. The game launches on May 22 for PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC, with a Switch 2 version planned but undated. If the trailer is any indication, this might be the most fun you can have with plastic bricks and a cape.
why_it_matters: The trailer shows how shared cultural memories—like a 90s hit song—can connect generations, suggesting that pop-culture products are increasingly designed to entertain both young people and their parents at the same time. It also highlights how games borrow from film and music history to create meaning beyond just gameplay, turning a simple ad into a talk-about moment that crosses age boundaries.

background_read: Seal’s 'Kiss from a Rose' was originally released in 1994 but became a global hit after being featured on the Batman Forever soundtrack in 1995, winning three Grammy Awards.
Batman Forever (1995), directed by Joel Schumacher and starring Val Kilmer, Jim Carrey (as the Riddler), and Tommy Lee Jones (as Two-Face), introduced a more colorful and campy take on Gotham.

The Arkham series of Batman games (by Rocksteady and WB Games Montréal) began with Arkham Asylum in 2009 and was praised for its gritty interpretation of the character, influencing many superhero games since.
TT Games is famous for adapting major film franchises like Star Wars, Harry Potter, and Marvel into Lego video games that balance humor with playful building mechanics.

The reference to Tommy Lee Jones allegedly hating Jim Carrey on set stems from behind-the-scenes stories where Jones reportedly told Carrey, 'I cannot sanction your buffoonery,' highlighting real tension that amused fans for decades.

perspectives.description: Fans of all ages see the song choice as a brilliant homage to Batman's entire media history, believing it proves the game respects older audiences while still being accessible to new players. The inclusion of an inside joke about Jim Carrey and Tommy Lee Jones feels like a reward for loyal fans, strengthening their connection to the franchise.

Some observers argue that relying on a 90s power ballad is a cheap trick to provoke nostalgia, masking a lack of original ideas. They worry that marketing leans too heavily on past cultural references rather than trusting a new product's own merits, which could set a disappointing standard for future game ads.

The choice fits a broader industry trend where cross-generational nostalgia is used to maximize commercial appeal, as seen in reboots, sequels, and adaptations that mine 80s and 90s properties. By layering references for different age groups, marketers create a 'shared family experience' that can boost sales without alienating any single demographic.

If this approach proves successful, future game trailers might become even more self-aware, deliberately incorporating obscure cultural call-backs for niche audiences. This could lead to a new genre of advertising that functions like an Easter egg hunt for fans, though developers will need to balance such winks with welcoming newcomers.
